hints.content:
##Strategy

Let's first find the indefinite integral $\displaystyle\int\sin(4x)\,dx\, $.  Then we can use the result to compute the definite integral.

##Finding the indefinite integral

To find $\displaystyle\int\sin(4x)\,dx\, $, we can use U-substitution.

If we let $\blueD {u=4x}$, then ${du=4 \, dx}$ and $\maroonD{ \,dx=\dfrac{1}{4}\, du}$.  

So we have:


$\begin{align}\displaystyle\int\sin(\blueD{4x})\,\maroonD{dx}\,
&=\displaystyle\int \sin(\blueD u)\cdot \maroonD{\dfrac14\, du}\,\\\\\\\\
&=\dfrac14\displaystyle\int\sin(u)\,du\\\\\\\\
&=\dfrac{1}{4}\cdot -\cos(u)+C\\\\\\\\
&=-\dfrac14\cos(4x)+C
\end{align}$

##Evaluating the definite integral

Now let's compute the definite integral:

$\begin{align}\displaystyle\int^{\pi/4}_{0}\sin(4x)\,dx\,&= -\dfrac14\cos(4x)\Bigg|^{\pi/4}_0\\\\\\\\
&=-\dfrac{1}{4}\left(\cos\left(4\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)-\cos(4\cdot 0)\right)\\\\\\\\
&=-\dfrac14(\cos(\pi)-\cos(0))\\\\\\\
&=-\dfrac14(-1-1)\\\\\\\\
&=\dfrac12\end{align}$

[[☃ explanation 1]]

options.explanation:
No, we could use U-substitution to calculate the definite integral directly. 

However, with this method, we must be sure to adjust our limits of integration.  

Here, when $\greenD{x=0}\,$, $\greenD{~u=0}~$ and when $~\goldD {x=\dfrac{\pi}{4}}\,$, $\goldD{u=\pi}\,$, so our limits of integration change respectively.

We can substitute to rewrite the definite integral as:

$\displaystyle\int^{\goldD{\pi/4}}_{\greenD0}\sin(4x)\,dx\, = \displaystyle\int^{\goldD \pi}_{\greenD 0}\sin( u)\cdot {\dfrac14\, du}\, $ 

We can now evaluate the definite integral as shown below:

$\begin{align}\displaystyle\int^{ \pi}_{ 0}\sin( u)\cdot {\dfrac14\, du}\, &=\dfrac14\displaystyle\int^{ \pi}_{ 0}\sin(u)\, du\, \\
\\\\\\
&=\dfrac14(-\cos(u))\Bigg|^{\pi}_0\\\\\\\\
&=-\dfrac14\Big(\cos(\pi)-\cos(0)\Big) \\\\\\\\
&=-\dfrac14(-1-1)\\\\\\\\
&=\dfrac12
\end{align}$
